chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: Now, if you recall from the beginning of the lesson, we talked about three major ways to estimate value. One is intrinsic value, which we just covered. Another is book value, which we're going to cover now. And the other is market capitalization.

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: So let's take a look at book value. Here's a classic definition of book value. It's total assets of the company. In other words, things like property that is owned and so on. Minus intangible assets and liabilities.

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: So intangible assets are things that are difficult to put a price on. They're things like the value of a brand or a patent or so on. Liabilities are a little bit easier to calculate. Those are just things like loans that are owed and so on. So let's consider what is the book value for an example company.

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: Let's say the company owns four factories and that each of these factories is worth about $10 million. These are assets and altogether they're worth about $40 million. Suppose this company also holds three very important patents and each patent is valued at about $5 million.

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: The value of these patents is about $15 million. But these are intangible assets that are hard to price exactly. Finally, suppose this company has one large loan. This would be under the liabilities column of $10 million. If we follow this rule that book values total assets.

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: So total assets are this 40 million plus the 15 million or 55 million. Minus intangible assets. So we just don't count these intangible assets. And liabilities. So all together, we've got our total assets minus intangible assets,

chunks.title: Book value
chunks.text: which is 40 million. And liabilities minus this 10 million. So in this case, this company's book value is 30 million.
